name: Tara Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining firms, technology companies or political groups, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a haul-truck crew and write the handover notes in a small blue book before anyone takes a vehicle out. I listen for a change in the engine and watch the ground near the loading face, because a clean checklist cannot show me every problem.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work gives you pride, and what part is hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when the newer drivers come back from a shift having learned the route without taking a risk. The rotation is tiring, but my pay is typical and my partner and I have about five months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the dispatch board sorted its routine notices better, I would try it after someone on the crew had checked it. I would still read my blue handover book and listen to the radio before sending a truck out. I would tell the crew that a quicker notice board can save time without changing who is responsible for the road. I would say to keep the old checks beside it until we know what it misses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving and crew checks look secure in this mild picture, and my savings cover several months. I am not eager to change a routine that works, but I would listen if the system proved itself on another shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same rotation and try the board only on the handover notes that match our radio log. My partner and I would keep our monthly savings transfer instead of spending it because a new screen looked useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a little uneasy about instructions arriving without anyone explaining them. I do not expect this small change to take my job, and five months of savings keeps the question from becoming an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop trusting a notice from the board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it missed a barricade or changed a route without a radio call, I would stop and check with the control room. I would write the error in my blue book and tell the next crew what happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the team that installed the board before using it on a night shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask them to show a real route change from our pit and explain where the information came from. If they could not explain that, I would keep using the paper handover until they could.

say: I would say a faster board can help while **our crew** keeps the road check.
I would keep old checks until **we** know what it misses.
think: I think **my driving work** looks secure in this mild picture.
Five months saved means I can **wait for proof**.
do: Keep the **current rotation** and compare board notices with radio logs.
Continue the **monthly savings transfer** with my partner.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about unexplained instructions, not about losing my job.
S0.quote: I would say to keep the old checks beside it until we know what it misses.
fieldNote: Tara accepts small changes after **crew verification**.
Her **five-month cushion** makes the mild change manageable.
The blue **handover book** is a practical record she already relies on.

steps.text: Keep the haul-truck rotation and compare board notices with the radio log
Continue the household monthly savings transfer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine may start with route planning, shift bookings and writing the maintenance notes. The truck is still hands-on, but as a team lead I do some of that desk work between shifts. I would tell people the planning tool is worth learning once the foreman has shown it working on a real route. I would also say the mine should explain whether the lead allowance changes when software takes over part of the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the driving part stays safer than the route and booking tasks, at least for now. I would not quit over a new board, but I would want a proven way to keep my lead hours if other crews are using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a trusted operator from the day shift to show me the planner before I use it on nights. If it works, I would learn the steps and keep my old route notes until the mine says which record becomes official.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the lead paperwork could change, though I do not expect the truck shifts to disappear first. My partner and I would postpone buying a used camper until we knew whether the lead allowance stayed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on your first pay slip after the planner starts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the lead allowance and overtime line with the previous month. If either changed, I would ask the foreman whether that was a trial adjustment or a lasting change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the planner gives your crew a route you would not use, how would you respond?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the road, the radio and the reason the planner gives before I accept it. Once another experienced operator had confirmed that the route was safe, I would use it and keep a note for the next handover.

say: I would learn the planner after a trusted operator **shows it working**.
I would ask whether **my lead allowance** changes with new software.
think: I think driving is safer than **planning tasks** for now.
I want proof the tool helps **me keep lead hours**.
do: Ask a day-shift operator to demonstrate the **route planner**.
Compare the next pay slip for a changed **lead allowance**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about lead paperwork, but not ready to leave the truck.
S1.quote: I would also say the mine should explain whether the lead allowance changes when software takes over part of the paperwork.
fieldNote: Tara is open to technology after **peer demonstration**.
She tracks the **lead allowance** rather than assuming the whole job is at risk.
A postponed camper purchase is a **conditional household decision**.

steps.text: Learn the route planner after a day-shift operator demonstrates it
Delay buying the used camper until lead pay is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would put thinking AI into the mine office by 2028 and robots into the pit around 2031. I could keep driving for a few years, but I do not know whether the mine would keep the same crew while it waited. I would tell the crew the planning work changes first and the hands-on robots follow about three years later. I would ask the mine to show us which jobs remain and which training places are actually funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is short notice for a new trade, but five months of savings gives me some room to ask questions. I would look at an apprenticeship with a real mechanic before paying for a course or trusting an online lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the maintenance foreman to let me watch one paid service shift and explain the apprenticeship route. In 2029, the first year after thinking AGI arrives, I would apply for a workshop place only if the job involved physical checks and a named wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the mine could change my hours before I finish learning, even though robots come later. I would keep our five months of savings intact and stop looking at the camper until I knew what the roster would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the workshop job is mostly records and planning that AGI can already do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would ask whether the mechanic still does physical checks and repairs before I call it a safer job. The records could go too, and I would need to see actual vacancies and pay instead of assuming a workshop is protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no paid apprenticeship were available in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving and ask the other local mines when they next take apprentices. If every offer meant unpaid study, I would not quit my job; I would keep saving until I found a place that paid me to learn.

say: I would tell the crew thinking AI comes first and robots follow **three years later**.
I would ask which training places are **funded before I enroll**.
think: I have five months saved, so I can **ask before moving**.
I know records work may go to **AGI**.
do: Watch one paid service shift and ask about the **apprenticeship route**.
In 2029, apply only for physical checks with a **named wage**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because hours could change before I finish learning.
S2.quote: The records could go too, and I would need to see actual vacancies and pay instead of assuming a workshop is protected.
fieldNote: Tara balances a short lead time against **five months of savings**.
She seeks a **paid apprenticeship** rather than self-funded online study.
Physical workshop work is a possibility, not a **guaranteed safe role**.

steps.text: Ask the maintenance foreman for a paid apprenticeship intake
Delay the used camper purchase until the roster is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me try a mechanical apprenticeship before the office work changes, and the robot date follows about three years after that. I would keep the truck job while I find out whether I am any good at maintenance. I would say there is time to train, but the mine should tell us what work it expects to need in 2031 and 2034. I would not promise the crew that three extra years means the same jobs and pay will remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer lead makes it easier for me to learn from a mechanic after a normal shift. I would need to know whether physical inspection work still has enough openings once robots are due, because I do not want another job that ends right after I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a paid trial apprenticeship over the next few years and ask for the course requirements in writing. In 2032, after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical inspection work only if it had a real wage and useful experience before the robots arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I have several years to prepare, but the mine has not said how many people it will keep. I would stay on the truck while I try maintenance and avoid giving up a steady wage just for a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you that the apprenticeship is worth doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see a mechanic's ordinary work and know how much of it is physical rather than records. I would also ask what apprentices earn and whether graduates have actually moved into paid inspection shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, if inspection jobs are few or end when robots arrive, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare openings at the other local mines and ask about maintenance work that uses the same skills. If none of those jobs had a clear wage beyond 2034, I would keep my truck license and continue saving while I looked.

say: I would say we have time to train, but the mine must share **staffing plans**.
I would not promise three extra years preserve the **same jobs and pay**.
think: I can learn maintenance **after a normal shift**.
I need to know if physical inspection has enough **lasting openings**.
do: Try a paid apprenticeship and get the **requirements in writing**.
In 2032, seek physical inspection work with **useful experience**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because I can prepare, but staffing is unknown.
S3.quote: I would not promise the crew that three extra years means the same jobs and pay will remain.
fieldNote: Tara sees the five-year lead as time to **test a trade**.
She asks whether **physical tasks and earnings** persist after robot arrival.
She will keep her **current wage** until training leads to a real role.

steps.text: Try a paid maintenance apprenticeship and get requirements in writing
Keep the truck job while checking inspection vacancies and pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me enough time to see whether maintenance suits me before thinking work changes in 2036. Robots come about three years later, so I would still want to know how long a physical job might last. I would tell the crew the long warning is useful if the mine pays people to learn a trade. I would not say a decade guarantees a job after 2039, because the hands-on machines are part of this picture too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I would still need a reliable wage, and ten years lets me test maintenance before committing. I would keep my savings at five months or better, because a training certificate is not a promise that a mine will hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try the apprenticeship with paid shifts and ask which employers hire graduates. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrives, I would check whether physical maintenance work still had vacancies and what the wage was before changing crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, not panicked, because I have years to test the trade and keep my savings steady. I would rather move after seeing a real job and a real wage than guess at what 2039 will bring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What facts would you need before accepting a maintenance job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what the job pays, whether it is mostly physical, and how many years the employer expects to need it. If robots were about to take the work, I would want to know that before I gave up a truck shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If that job had no clear future beyond 2039, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the haul-truck job while it was available and ask the other mines about their apprenticeships. I would not leave steady pay for a short contract without enough time to find the next job.

say: I would ask the mine for **paid training** during the long lead.
I would not treat a decade as a **guaranteed job after 2039**.
think: At 37, I still need a **reliable wage**.
I would check whether a certificate helps **an employer hire me**.
do: Try paid apprenticeship shifts and check **graduate hiring**.
In 2037, compare physical vacancies and **wages** before changing crews.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with time to test a trade and keep saving.
S4.quote: I would rather move after seeing a real job and a real wage than guess at what 2039 will bring.
fieldNote: Tara treats the decade as a chance to **test maintenance**.
She wants **physical work and pay** details before committing.
She will not give up **steady pay** for an uncertain short contract.

steps.text: Try paid apprenticeship shifts and ask employers about graduate hiring
Keep the truck shift until a maintenance job names pay and duration

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time to learn before the mine changes its planning work. Paid apprenticeship hours and a clear account of actual openings would help me decide whether maintenance is a sound step.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I am willing to learn when someone shows me the job and the pay at the end. I want a useful skill I can take to another mine, not a course that only teaches me to click a different screen.

headlineQuote: I am willing to learn when someone shows me the job and the pay at the end.
portrait: Tara Ziegler is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
She is highly skilled, earns **typical pay** and shares expenses with her partner.
The household has about **five months** of expenses saved.
She uses technology once it has worked for **other crews**.
She favors **paid apprenticeships** and a skill that can travel to another mine.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to adjust lead duties before planning tasks change.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeship hours** and clear information about actual openings would help Tara choose a sound next step.
